excerpts.text: I built and own the release system for the company's standard machine and container images. I replaced a single, fully baked image stream with layered images, where each application's metadata picks its runtime and CPU architecture. Shipping a new runtime went from days of coordination across teams to one pipeline run.
The old model baked a single image stream: one Java and Tomcat version, and no ARM support. Every application got the same runtime, and releasing a new one took days of coordination across teams.
Every build also did the full bake, so developers waited for it even on small changes.

I own the platform's machine image ( AMI ) and container image release systems: the Packer builds, the release metadata, sharing released images with the other AWS accounts, and runtime support. I built the layered model on this page, which shipped in mid-2025.

A sibling platform team was building the company's new standard delivery pipeline at the same time. I worked with them to add runtime- and architecture-specific image selection to it before launch, so application teams moved to both in one migration instead of two. Then I led onboarding sessions for every business domain.
Layered runtime images, from metadata to applications

Metadata. Each application declares its runtime, version and CPU architecture. The platform supports several Java, Tomcat and Node versions on two Amazon Linux releases, for both x86 and ARM (Graviton), and keeps the two previous versions alongside the current one. One pipeline. The pipeline reads the metadata and builds the image layers the application asks for. Two kinds of build. Snapshot builds skip the application bake, so feedback comes back fast while a team is developing. They are never promoted. Release builds do the full bake and run Python (pytest) tests inside the image. Promotion gate. A release is promoted only with a green bake and a clean security scan, or an approved exception. Shared across accounts. The release is shared with the AWS accounts that use it, and tags record its lineage. Releases move from snapshot to release to stable to deprecated. Stable keeps the previous version for rollback, and pulled images are quarantined. Reaching applications. Containers pick up new releases through moving release tags and an automated patching operator, in monthly patch groups. EC2 applications are rebaked and rolled by a shared patch pipeline.

Bakes start automatically every month. I make the remediation and promotion decisions for these images: fix and rebake, or defer with a time-boxed exception, and I force an out-of-cycle release when a critical finding lands mid-month. The security team owns the scanners and approves exceptions.
The main choice was to make the runtime part of each application's metadata, so one pipeline builds whatever the application asks for.
Adding a runtime then means adding a supported option, not building and maintaining another pipeline. A team can move to a newer version, or onto ARM, by changing its metadata.

The second choice was splitting builds in two. Most builds during development don't need a fully baked image, so snapshot builds skip that step and come back fast. Only release builds pay for the full bake, the tests and the scan, and only they get promoted.
A new runtime release went from days of coordination across teams to one pipeline run.
Snapshot builds made everyday build-to-deploy feedback several times faster.
Teams can choose their runtime version and run on ARM (Graviton) instances, which the old model didn't support.
Application teams moved to the new images and the new delivery pipeline in a single migration.

A security fix needed a newer database driver. The uploaded package had the right version number but the wrong contents: it was an installer, not the driver. The bake passed, and so did the scan, because both trusted the version. I found it by inspecting what was inside the package, then swapped in the correct artifact. The lesson I took: version-based checks can't catch wrong contents, so assert the contents before promotion.
After a migration, the automatic monthly trigger for bakes had quietly gone missing. I found it and restored it.
I also led a round of work on bake reliability and reporting: handling scanner rate limits, auditing triggers and consolidating failure reports.
I also wrote the scheduled part of the shared patch pipeline that rebakes and rolls EC2 applications each month, in Python .

A shared deployment path for EC2 and EKS services. Each release starts as a new copy beside the live one and must pass health checks before it takes any live traffic. Traffic then moves over in approved steps, and a person can roll back at any step.
The company's standard delivery platform runs hundreds of production deployments a day, for teams across the company.

At that volume, some releases will be bad. A service won't start, or it can't reach something it depends on. The deployment path has to expect that and make the safe outcome the default, so a bad release fails in the pipeline instead of in front of customers.
This is a team system. A sibling platform team created the company's standard delivery pipeline .
On that pipeline, I built the shared build stage and the delivery paths for AWS Lambda and AWS Bedrock AgentCore . The AgentCore path has its own page .
I co-developed the EC2 and EKS paths on this page with the rest of my platform team: the health gating, approvals, traffic shifting and rollback. I was one of several engineers on them.
I also wrote the Open Policy Agent policies in Harness that moved non-compliant pipelines on the standard path from warnings to hard blocks, as the legacy pipelines are retired.
A health-gated blue-green rollout, step by step

Build. The shared build stage produces the release. Start the new copy. The release starts as a new copy of the service (green) beside the live one (blue). No live traffic goes to it. Health gate. Green has to pass health checks before any live traffic reaches it. If it fails, the rollout stops there, and live traffic never moved. Approval. A person approves each traffic step. Shift traffic. The Application Load Balancer moves a share of traffic to green. Steps 4 and 5 repeat until all traffic is on green. Done. With every step approved, green becomes the live version.
A rollback starts when a person rejects a traffic step or asks for one. Traffic then returns to the last healthy version, and the rollback is built to finish without manual work.
Tools: Harness runs the pipeline, Application Load Balancers shift the traffic, and the services run on EC2 or Amazon EKS .

The main design choice is where automation stops. Health checks before traffic are automatic. Moving to the next traffic step, or rolling back, is a person's decision, and once someone decides to roll back, the rollback runs on its own. Nothing promotes a release automatically from live metrics, which is why I call this a progressive rollout with approval gates rather than a canary.

The reasoning: checks that run before traffic catch the failures that are cheap to detect, like a release that won't start or fails its health endpoint, and they cost customers nothing. Automated promotion needs trustworthy signals for each service and enough traffic to judge them. Across many teams running very different services, those signals vary a lot, so a person who knows the service, watching its own dashboards, is the simpler gate for each step.

Starting a full new copy instead of replacing the live one in place has a cost: two copies run during a rollout. In return, the live version is untouched until the new one has shown it can run, and going back is a routing change rather than a redeploy.
Most production deployments run through the standard path. The rest run on separate legacy pipelines that are being retired.
On EC2 , the gate waits for the new instances to report healthy. On EKS , it waits for the new pods to reach a steady state. Both happen before the load balancer sends green any live traffic.
Only one rollout runs per service and environment at a time. A deployment lock enforces it, so two pipeline runs can't fight over the same load balancer.

Suppose a pipeline times out right after asking the load balancer to shift traffic. Its own record says the shift was requested, but nobody knows whether it was applied. Reversing the step blindly can make things worse. The safer recovery reads the load balancer's actual state, decides which version should be live, moves routing to match, and only then lets the next rollout start. My rule of thumb for any deployment system: trust the observed state over the pipeline's memory of what it asked for.

For services with steady traffic, I would add automated analysis of error rates and latency between steps, as a second signal next to the human approval. For low-traffic services I would keep the human gate on its own, because there isn't enough traffic to judge automatically.

I built the company's self-service developer platform end to end. One workflow sets up everything a new service needs to ship: its code repository, container registry, Kubernetes namespace and deployment pipeline, with no routine manual work from the platform team.
It covers a broad catalog of infrastructure and is used by many teams across the company.

Every new service needs the same groundwork: somewhere for its code, somewhere for its container images, a place to run, and a pipeline to deploy it. If each piece is a separate request to the platform team, every new service starts with a wait, and every team sets it up a little differently. With many teams shipping services, that groundwork has to be self-service and come out right by default.
I built the platform end to end.

Much of the newer self-service infrastructure is built from reusable AWS CDK constructs and stacks. I wrote constructs for Application Load Balancers, a web application firewall that blocks by default, Lambda authorizers, Network Load Balancers and container registries. I also built the self-service workflow teams use to create Application Load Balancers, and I'm extending it to listener rules and target groups.

When a team arrives with a new design, I often represent the platform. I lead the session, map their stack to the patterns the platform supports, work out what it needs for infrastructure, security, networking, observability, identity and deployment, split the work between teams, write the platform stories, and follow through until it runs in production on a supported setup.
On the delivery side, I wrote the policy-as-code rules that block non-compliant pipelines. That part is on the deployments page .
The self-service flow, from request to deployable service

Request. A team picks what it needs from a self-service catalog. One workflow. It creates the whole set together: the code repository, the container registry, the Kubernetes namespace and the deployment pipeline. Ship. The new service deploys through the company's standard delivery pipeline . More of the same. The catalog offers other infrastructure, such as Application Load Balancers, self-served the same way.
The main choice was to create everything a new service needs in one workflow.

The four pieces only work together: the pipeline needs the registry, and the deployment needs the namespace. Creating them in one pass means names, permissions and settings line up from the start, and nobody has to stitch them together by hand or file one request after another.
The platform covers a broad catalog of infrastructure and is used by many teams across the company, without routine manual work from the platform team.

I primarily drove a spec-driven, self-service platform for API Gateway that replaced a process built on Jenkins , custom CDK and manual deploys. To wire integrations into a team's API spec, I explored five approaches in my own branches; the one we chose shipped as the self-service platform's integration-wiring page.

I built parts of the stack and construct code: loading specs from S3, VPC Link wiring, VPC endpoint and hosted-zone discovery, mutual TLS, the HTTP integration mode, an OpenAPI-only mode and base path mappings. I also ran the migration from the old process: the field mapping, the changes that would break a deploy, and walking the first team through it.

While researching the old process, I found why API stages kept falling out of CloudFormation 's tracking: each deploy generated only the stage it targeted, with a retain policy, so every other stage was dropped from the stack. I confirmed the new design avoids it, worked through the relevant CloudFormation limits (resource counts, template size, stage ceilings), and scoped the follow-up work.

A team arrived with a multi-tier AWS application. I turned their design into platform requirements and helped take an optional web application firewall for load balancers from a security draft to a supported option on the existing platform stack. I shaped and sequenced the stories, agreed the production blocking posture with the security team, reviewed the construct and stack changes, and supported that team as the first to run it in production. I didn't design their application.

I built the path that takes AI agents on AWS Bedrock AgentCore to production. It provisions the AgentCore infrastructure with CDK , builds the agent's image, tests each new version in stages and promotes it through the company's standard pipeline. Every production agent at the company ships through it.
Several teams run agents in production on it.
AgentCore was new: we had early access to it with AWS , before it was generally available.

A few SDK calls and a script can deploy an agent for a demo, but a production agent needs what any production service gets: a repeatable build, testing before it takes real traffic, a controlled promotion, and the same access and security rules as everything else. Without one shared path, every team would work all of that out alone, on a service that was still changing under them.

I took the deployment path from design, while AgentCore was still in preview with AWS , to production. I built the CDK stacks for AgentCore Runtime and Gateway, onboarding through the self-service platform, the image bake , staged validation, gated promotion, and the check that the live version is the one we shipped.
I also wrote the AgentCore log forwarding and set the platform's IAM role naming convention for AgentCore Gateway.
Another team builds the agent template that teams start from. I drove its platform requirements.

To get teams started, I led eight two-hour, hands-on sessions, one for each business domain, on what the platform is and how to onboard an agent. The platform sections were mine; the template team presented its own.
I own the infrastructure and the delivery path. The agents themselves, and their code, belong to the teams that build them.
Shipping an AgentCore agent, step by step

Onboard. A team registers its agent through the self-service platform. Provision. CDK stacks create the AgentCore Runtime and Gateway. Build. The standard pipeline bakes the agent's image. Validate in stages. The new version runs on a staging endpoint and is tested there first. Promote. A gate promotes the tested version to production. Verify. The pipeline confirms the live endpoint is serving the new version.
The main choice was to treat an agent like any other production service: one productized path, defined as code, that every agent ships through, instead of per-team scripts.
The service was new and still changing. With one path, the platform absorbs each change once instead of every team chasing it, and security and operations have one place to look.
Every production AgentCore agent at the company ships through this path. None uses the old SDK and script route.
Several teams run agents in production on it, many with more than one.

AgentCore itself runs each session in its own isolated micro-VM and provides versioned endpoints. On top of that, the platform sets up a least-privilege model with three separate identities (the user, the agent's own role, and the identity it uses to call other systems), guardrails at the organization and application level, a three-tier evaluation setup, OpenTelemetry instrumentation, and the staged test-and-promote flow above.
I build and run the company's Kubernetes platform with my team: a Fargate-only EKS estate spread across many AWS accounts.
I refactored the cluster Terraform so a new cluster takes hours instead of weeks, and I built the cluster monitoring with Prometheus and Grafana.

Many teams run their services on Kubernetes . Every cluster has to look the same, come up quickly when a new one is needed, and be easy to see into when something goes wrong, without anyone hand-building or hand-checking each one.

I build and run the EKS estate with my platform team. Each cluster runs the same platform extensions: the AWS Load Balancer Controller, cert-manager, external-dns, Fluent Bit , kube-prometheus with Thanos and Grafana, a cost exporter and in-house operators.

I refactored the cluster Terraform to cut provisioning from weeks to under two hours. I delivered a production cluster against a one-week deadline, and in 2026 I stood up a new pair of clusters end to end.

I built the cluster monitoring with Prometheus and Grafana, including the cluster extensions and dashboards. I also work on Thanos, including an upgrade that fixed an instance-metadata issue, and on Alertmanager's routing.
How an EKS cluster is created and run

Define. Reusable Terraform modules define a cluster and its platform extensions. One run. A single Terraform run creates the cluster, the same way every time. Run on Fargate . Every workload runs on Fargate, so there are no worker nodes to manage. Platform extensions. Each cluster gets the same set: traffic (the AWS Load Balancer Controller, cert-manager, external-dns), logs ( Fluent Bit ) and metrics (Prometheus, with Thanos and Grafana, and Alertmanager for alerts). Monthly patching. Containers pick up patched base images every month through moving release tags and an automated patching operator. That flow is on the runtime images page .
Container registries and other container resources are separate: they ship on every merge to the infrastructure repository.

The main change was making a new cluster one repeatable Terraform run. I replaced cluster-specific code with reusable modules, folded the steps people used to do by hand into the run, and fixed the failures that used to stall it, such as dependency cycles and credentials expiring partway through.
A new cluster takes hours instead of weeks.
Every cluster comes with the same monitoring, so a problem in one looks the same as a problem in any other.
Investigations usually start from CloudWatch, CloudTrail and OpenSearch , then move to load balancer, session and Systems Manager logs, and network and identity telemetry as needed.
